dok_rationale: Part (c) weighs competing claims using the day's numerical or graphical evidence and explains a limitation or consequence; the judgment requires linked reasoning beyond a calculation.
stem: Suppose a coin advertised as fair is flipped 10 times and gives HHHHHHTTTT. To investigate what chance alone could produce, a class simulates 100 sets of 10 independent fair-coin flips. For each set, the class records the longest run of matching outcomes; the frequency table shows the results.\par\smallskip \textbf{Claim A:} ``The coin is rigged---six heads in a row cannot be chance.''\par \textbf{Claim B:} ``Streaks like this can happen by chance; simulation can tell us how unusual this one is.''
first_take: Which claim seems better supported right now? Cite one detail from the sequence or table.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State the longest run in the observed sequence and the most common longest run in the simulated sets.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Estimate the chance of a run at least as long as the observed one. Use the number of simulated sets with such a run divided by 100.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Which claim is better supported? Use the simulation count and explain why it does not prove the coin is fair. To improve the estimate, describe one trial, what you would count, and why you would repeat many trials. Write 3--4 sentences.

answers.a: The observed sequence has a longest run of 6, the six consecutive heads. In the simulated sets, 3 is the most common longest-run value, appearing 32 times.
answers.b: Seven of the 100 simulated sets have a longest run of at least 6, so the estimate is $7/100=0.07$. In context, about 7 percent of sets of 10 independent flips from a fair coin produced a run at least as long as the observed run in this simulation.
answers.c: Claim B is better supported: 7 of 100 fair-coin trials had a run at least 6 long, so the pattern can occur by chance. This result does not prove the actual coin is fair. One trial should use 10 independent fair-coin flips, recording the longest run of either outcome and counting a success when it is at least 6. Repeat many trials, such as 10,000, to reduce the chance variation in the estimated proportion.

expectedElements.description: Chooses B with 7 of 100 and avoids claiming proof of fairness
Matches one trial to 10 independent fair-coin flips and counts a longest run of at least 6
Explains why many repetitions improve the estimate

scoringGuide.E: Includes all three required reasoning elements above, with correct contextual evidence.
scoringGuide.P: Includes at least one substantive correct reasoning link above, but omits or misstates another required element.
scoringGuide.I: Includes no substantive correct reasoning link above; an unsupported choice or copied number alone is insufficient.

commonMistakes: Treating a run of six as impossible because each individual sequence is unlikely
Using six flips rather than reproducing all 10 flips in one trial
Counting only runs of exactly 6 and discarding longer runs
Claiming that 7 percent proves the coin is fair
